cases.title: Quran 65:4: a divorce waiting period for wives 'who have not yet menstruated'
cases.claim: Quran 65:4 legislates the iddah (post-divorce waiting period) for three groups of wives, including those 'who have not menstruated' — and the classical commentators (Tabari, Ibn Kathir, and the standard tafsir tradition) uniformly read this as girls who have not yet reached puberty. Since Quran 33:49 says no iddah exists at all for an unconsummated marriage, the verse presupposes consummated marriages to prepubescent girls. This embeds child marriage in the Quran's own divorce legislation — independent of the Aisha biography.

sources.name: Tafsir Ibn Kathir on 65:4
Ma'arif al-Qur'an on 65:4
Discover The Truth — 'Quran 65:4 – The Child Marriage Claim' (Muslim response)
Sahih al-Bukhari 5134

cases.response: Modern apologists argue 'those who have not menstruated' refers to adult women with delayed menarche or amenorrhea, not children, and that the verse addresses waiting periods generally without endorsing child marriage; some add that a marriage contract does not imply consummation.

responseSource.name: Modern apologetic (e.g., Discover The Truth); contrast the classical position in Ibn Kathir and Ma'arif al-Qur'an, which state the verse covers 'the young who have not reached the years of menstruation'

cases.rationale: The delayed-menarche reading is a modern retrofit held by no classical authority — the tafsir tradition is unanimous that the clause covers the not-yet-pubescent, and the fiqh manuals of all four schools drew the corresponding rule. The iddah logic is the trap: 33:49 removes any waiting period for unconsummated marriages, so an iddah for the never-menstruated only has work to do if such marriages were consummated. This is the legislative twin of the Aisha case: even if every biographical report were discarded, the law remains in the text.

cases.title: Four witnesses: the evidence standard that turned rape victims into defendants
cases.claim: Quran 24:4 requires four eyewitnesses to prove unlawful intercourse, on pain of eighty lashes for the accuser, and 24:13 applies the same test. Classical fiqh folded rape (zina-bil-jabr) into zina's evidentiary rules, and when Pakistan codified this in the 1979 Hudood Ordinance, the documented result was rape victims prosecuted for zina — their complaint treated as a confession of intercourse they could not prove was forced. It took secular legislation, the Women's Protection Act of 2006, to move rape back out of the sharia framework into the Penal Code.

sources.name: Offence of Zina (Enforcement of Hudood) Ordinance 1979 — text and commentary, Harvard Islamic Law Blog
'Twenty-Five Years of Hudood Ordinances — A Review', Washington & Lee Law Review
Women's Protection Bill (2006) — Wikipedia
Al Jazeera — 'Pakistan compromises on rape law' (2006)

cases.response: Muslims respond that 24:4's original purpose was protective — shielding women (occasioned by the slander of Aisha) from casual accusations of adultery; that rape could alternatively be prosecuted as hiraba (violent crime) without four witnesses; and that the Hudood Ordinance was bad man-made legislation, not true sharia — as shown by Pakistani religious scholars who supported the 2006 reform.

responseSource.name: Reformist and traditional jurists as surveyed in the Washington & Lee Law Review article and the 2006 reform debate

cases.rationale: The protective-intent point about slander is genuine and should be conceded — but the case is about downstream application: the classical manuals did apply zina's evidentiary bar to rape claims, the hiraba route was the minority workaround rather than the operative rule, and when a modern state implemented the classical framework, the predicted injustice occurred at scale for 27 years. The instructive contrast is Deuteronomy 22:25-27, which explicitly declares the rape victim innocent ('to the young woman you shall do nothing') with no witness quota imposed on her. Usage note: lead with the Pakistan history, which is documented, and acknowledge 24:4's anti-slander context up front — it makes the argument stronger, not weaker.

cases.title: Satan: angel or jinn? The exception that breaks the sentence
cases.claim: Five times the Quran says the angels were commanded to prostrate to Adam 'and they prostrated, except Iblis' (2:34; 7:11; 15:30-31; 20:116; 38:73-74) — grammar that counts Iblis among the angels. But 18:50 says 'he was of the jinn, so he rebelled.' The Quran also says angels never disobey Allah (66:6), yet on the angel reading Iblis did exactly that; and Iblis says he was created from fire (7:12), while the hadith says angels were created from light (Muslim 2996).
hadith: Sahih Muslim 2996 (angels created from light, jinn from smokeless fire)

sources.name: 'Iblis is not an Angel…' — survey of classical tafsir on 2:34
'The nature of Iblis in the Qur'an as interpreted by the commentators' — University of Malta
Bilal Ali Ansari — 'The Question of Fallen Angels and the Nature of Iblis'
Answering Islam — 'Is Satan an Angel or a Jinn?'

cases.response: Three classical harmonizations: (1) al-Tabari, following Ibn Abbas reports — Iblis belonged to a tribe of angels called 'jinn,' guardians of Paradise created from fire; (2) Hasan al-Basri, cited approvingly by Ibn Kathir — Iblis 'was not an angel for the twinkling of an eye,' and the exception in 2:34 is a 'disconnected exception' (he was merely among the angels when the command came); (3) al-Baydawi — created an angel, became jinn by deed.

responseSource.name: Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir (via al-Hasan al-Basri), al-Baydawi — as surveyed in the tafsir literature above

cases.rationale: The tradition never settled it, and the rescues are mutually exclusive: Tabari's 'angelic tribe called jinn' preserves the grammar of 2:34 but collides with 66:6 (angels cannot disobey) and the light/fire distinction; Hasan al-Basri's 'never an angel' saves 18:50 by making the Quran's own repeated sentence structure misleading five times over. In conversation this is a clean, self-contained internal-consistency test that requires no external sources — just the Quran read carefully. Pick either horn and let the tafsir tradition supply the contradiction.

cases.title: Six days or eight? The arithmetic of Surah 41
cases.claim: Four passages say the heavens and earth were created in six days (7:54; 10:3; 11:7; 25:59). But 41:9-12 itemizes: the earth in two days, then (thumma) mountains and provisions in four days, then (thumma) the seven heavens in two days — 2 + 4 + 2 = 8. Bonus tension: in 41:9-12 the earth is completed before the heavens, while 79:27-30 builds the heaven first and spreads the earth 'after that' (ba'da dhalika).

sources.name: IslamQA 31865 — 'Were the Heavens and Earth Created in 6 or 8 Days?'
Answering Islam — 'Six or eight days of creation?'
The Dawah Script — Surah 41:9-12 dialogue treatment

cases.response: The standard answer (IslamQA, following Ibn Kathir): the 'four days' of 41:10 are inclusive — the earth was created in two days and its mountains and provisions in two more, 'four days' meaning four in total up to that point. So 4 + 2 = 6.
cases.rationale: The inclusive reading has to fight the text's own conjunction: each stage is introduced with thumma ('then'), which in Arabic marks sequence, not overlap — nobody reads 'I built the house in two days, then finished the roof in four days' as six days total only by special pleading. Translators sympathetic to the harmonization must insert parenthetical glosses ('four days including the former two') that are not in the Arabic. Note honestly if raised: Christians read Genesis's days in more than one way too — but Genesis's numbers at least add up.

cases.title: Qadar: 'We have created for Hell many jinn and men'
cases.claim: The Quran teaches that Allah decrees everything including belief and disbelief: 'We have created for Hell many of the jinn and mankind' (7:179); 'whomever Allah leaves astray, none can guide' (7:178); 'nothing will befall us except what Allah has decreed for us' (9:51); 'you do not will unless Allah wills' (76:30; 81:29). In Sahih al-Bukhari 6594 the angel writes each person's deeds and whether he is 'doomed or blessed' before birth, and Bukhari 6596 is titled 'The pen has dried.' Allah creates people for Hell and then punishes them for what He decreed.

sources.name: Sahih al-Bukhari 6594 — the angel writes doomed or blessed
Sahih al-Bukhari 6596 — 'The pen has become dry'
IslamQA 264354 — 'Reconciling the Divine Decree and Free Will'
Abu Amina Elias — 'Pens have dried upon Allah's decree'

cases.response: Sunni orthodoxy answers with the Ash'ari doctrine of kasb ('acquisition'): Allah creates every act, but the human 'acquires' it and so bears responsibility; foreknowledge-writing is not compulsion; and 32:13 ('had We willed, We could have given every soul its guidance') shows guidance withheld justly. IslamQA frames it as a matter where reason must submit: both decree and responsibility are affirmed without full reconciliation.
cases.rationale: Kasb re-labels the problem rather than solving it — Muslim scholars themselves proverbially listed al-Ash'ari's kasb among the famously unintelligible doctrines, and the Quran's language is stronger than mere foreknowledge: created FOR Hell (7:179), 'I will surely fill Hell' (32:13), Allah 'sends astray whom He wills' (14:4). The biblical contrast is the point for conversation: the God of Scripture 'takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked' (Ezek 33:11), 'desires all people to be saved' (1 Tim 2:4), and pleads 'choose life' (Deut 30:19). Christians debating sovereignty and freedom do so inside those constraints; the Quran removes them. Handle with care: a Muslim may quote Calvinist material back — the answer is that no Christian tradition teaches God delights in damnation or creates men in order to damn them.

cases.title: Triple talaq and halala: the divorce that requires another man first
cases.claim: Quran 2:230: after a third divorce a woman is not lawful to her husband again 'until she has married another husband.' Muhammad applied it literally: when Rifa'a's thrice-divorced wife wanted to return to him, he answered, 'No — not until he tastes your sweetness and you taste his sweetness' (Bukhari 5260), i.e., the intervening marriage must be consummated. The rule generated halala/tahleel — arranged one-night marriages to re-legalize a wife — a practice still sold as a service today, and instant triple talaq remained live law until Muslim-majority jurisdictions legislated against it (India: struck down in Shayara Bano, 2017; criminalized 2019).

sources.name: Sahih al-Bukhari 5260
IslamQA 159041 — reconciling the hadiths forbidding tahleel with the wife of Rifa'a
Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017) — case summary
Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019 — Wikipedia

cases.response: Muslims respond that (1) contracted halala — marrying with the prior intention of divorcing to re-legalize the woman — is itself cursed and invalid in the hadith (the muhallil, 'the one who makes lawful,' is condemned; see IslamQA 159041); (2) the 2:230 rule is a deterrent designed to make men take divorce seriously; and (3) instant triple talaq in one sitting (talaq-e-biddat) is a condemned innovation, not original Islam.

responseSource.name: IslamQA 159041; mainstream Sunni fiqh on tahleel

cases.rationale: The curse on the muhallil only forbids the arrangement being explicit — the underlying rule stands on any reading: a thrice-divorced woman cannot return to her husband until another man has consummated a marriage with her, and Bukhari 5260 puts the consummation requirement in Muhammad's own mouth. The 'deterrent' framing concedes the mechanism: the deterrent's payload is the wife's sexual union with another man. The clandestine halala-service market (documented by the BBC in the UK, and litigated in India) is the rule's predictable equilibrium, and it took a secular constitutional court, over the opposition of the All India Muslim Personal Law Board, to kill the trigger practice. Contrast Jesus: divorce concessions exist 'because of your hardness of heart,' with no ritual requiring the woman's body as the price of reconciliation.

cases.title: The missing basmala: Uthman's editorial guess at Surah 9
cases.claim: Surah 9 (al-Tawbah/Bara'ah) is the only one of 114 surahs lacking the bismillah heading. Asked why, Uthman explained (Jami at-Tirmidhi 3086) that al-Anfal came early in Medina, Bara'ah late, its subject matter resembled al-Anfal's, and the Prophet died without clarifying whether it was part of it — 'so I put them adjacent and did not write the basmala between them.' The caliph who standardized the Quran describes a surah boundary settled by his own inference, not by revelation.

sources.name: Jami at-Tirmidhi 3086
IslamQA 173672 — 'Why There Is No Bismillah in Surah At-Tawbah'
Abu Amina Elias — why bismillah is missing from Surat al-Tawbah
The House of Wisdom — 'Surah Tawbah - No Basmalah?'

cases.response: The common devotional answer: the basmala (mercy formula) was deliberately omitted because al-Tawbah opens with a declaration of war and the repudiation of treaties — a surah of the sword needs no invocation of mercy (a view attributed to Ali). Others hold the surah order and boundaries were fixed by the Prophet's instruction (tawqifi), and Uthman's account is graded variously (Darussalam: hasan; some later critics weaken it).

responseSource.name: IslamQA 173672 and classical opinions surveyed there

cases.rationale: The two traditional answers undercut each other: if the omission were a revealed judgment about mercy and war, Uthman would not have explained it as his own uncertainty about where one surah ends and another begins. Weakness stated plainly: Tirmidhi 3086's grading is contested (hasan per Darussalam, weakened by some) — so use this as corroboration inside the compilation story, not as your lead; the site's uthman-burning and compilation cases carry the primary weight. The undisputed core is untouched by the grading dispute: the basmala is missing, the companion codices ordered surahs differently, and the arrangement of the mushaf passed through post-Muhammad editorial decisions.

cases.title: Haman in Pharaoh's Egypt: the Esther villain a thousand years early
cases.claim: The Quran places a figure named Haman in Egypt as Pharaoh's officer at the time of Moses (28:6, 28:8, 28:38; 29:39; 40:24, 40:36-37) — even having Pharaoh ask Haman to fire bricks and build a lofty tower to look upon the God of Moses. But Haman is the vizier of the Persian king in the Book of Esther, set roughly a millennium after Moses; and the tower-to-heaven motif belongs to Babel (Genesis 11), where baked bricks are likewise specified. The Quran reads like a fusion of Esther's villain with the Babel story, relocated to Egypt — exactly the blend already circulating in Jewish midrashic storytelling.

sources.name: Adam J. Silverstein, 'Haman' (Princeton University Press)
Silverstein, 'Haman in the Qur'an' — chapter in 'Veiling Esther, Unveiling Her Story' (Oxford)
Islamic Awareness — 'Biblical Haman, Qur'anic Haman' (the hmn-h defense)
Jewish Review of Books — 'Haman, Builder of Towers, Brother of Abraham?'

cases.response: Two Muslim defenses: (1) the Quranic Haman is simply a different Egyptian with a similar name; (2) the 'scientific miracle' version (popularized from Maurice Bucaille, developed by Islamic Awareness): 'hmn-h' appears in an Egyptian name catalogue as a chief of stone-quarry workers, so the Quran preserves an authentic Egyptian name lost to history.
cases.rationale: The hmn-h argument dissolves on inspection: it rests on reading a German-transliterated entry in a name lexicon, the reconstructed vocalization is conjectural, no Egyptologist endorses 'Haman' as an Egyptian name, and the alleged quarry-chief has no connection to Moses' era or to a vizier role. Meanwhile the academic treatment (Silverstein, no Christian apologist) concludes both Hamans are the same folkloric villain migrating between the Persian and Pharaonic courts via Near Eastern narrative fluidity — a frame that concedes precisely what the dictation-from-heaven model cannot afford: the Quran inherited a literary character, complete with Babel's bricks and tower, and set him in the wrong court. Pairs naturally with the site's Samaritan-anachronism and Dhul-Qarnayn cases as a third independent instance of the same pattern.

cases.title: The fly's wing, camel urine, and black seed: prophetic medicine vs. the miracle-of-science claim
cases.claim: Dawah routinely claims Muhammad's words anticipate modern science. The sahih medical corpus is the test: dip the fly in your drink because one wing carries the disease and the other its cure (Bukhari 3320); the tribesmen of Ukl/Urayna were prescribed camel milk and camel urine as medicine (Bukhari 233; 5686); black seed is 'a healing for every disease except death' (Bukhari 5688). A source reliable enough to establish embryology miracles is reliable enough to own these.

sources.name: Sahih al-Bukhari 3320 — the fly hadith
Sahih al-Bukhari 5686 — camel urine as medicine
Sahih al-Bukhari 5688 — black seed heals every disease
ICRAA — 'The Hadith of the Fly: Muslim Perspectives on Scientific Assessment'
Camel urine — Wikipedia (WHO advisory)

cases.response: Three defenses circulate: (1) vindication-by-study — a small 2021 Saudi-affiliated study on fly-wing dipping and assorted camel-urine papers are cited as confirmation; (2) reclassification — prophetic medical statements are worldly opinion, not revelation, per the date-pollination hadith ('you know better the affairs of your world,' Muslim 2363); (3) black seed's 'every disease' is idiomatic hyperbole for broad benefit.

responseSource.name: ICRAA and mainstream dawah treatments of the fly hadith

cases.rationale: The defenses cannot all be held at once, and each costs something: the vindication studies are small, fringe-journal, and post-hoc (and the WHO warns against camel urine consumption — a live issue during MERS); the worldly-opinion escape hatch contradicts how the statements are framed (categorical disease etiology, delivered as authoritative teaching and preserved in the Sahih's medicine chapters); and once 'every disease except death' is hyperbole, the method that finds precise embryology in equally loose language collapses. Usage note: deploy this as a response when the scientific-miracles claim is made — as a cold-open attack it reads as mockery and closes the conversation.

cases.title: Adam was sixty cubits tall — and people have been shrinking since
cases.claim: Bukhari 3326: 'Allah created Adam, making him 60 cubits tall' (roughly 27-30 meters / 90 feet), ending: 'people have been decreasing in stature since Adam's creation.' Both clauses are empirically testable and false: no giant human remains exist, and the skeletal record runs the other way — average stature has increased in recent centuries, and no ancient population approached even 3 meters.

sources.name: Sahih al-Bukhari 3326
IslamQA 22058 — 'Man was created tall then he kept getting shorter'
Let Me Turn The Tables — Muslim treatment of the height hadith
FaithAlone.net — 'Scientific Errors in Islam: The Size of Adam'

cases.response: IslamQA affirms the hadith literally and treats the fossil/archaeological objection as inconclusive. Others follow a suggestion that the 60-cubit height applies to Adam in Paradise or to people in Paradise ('whoever enters Paradise will be in the form of Adam'), not to earthly humans. Notably, Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani in Fath al-Bari already flagged the problem in the 15th century: the dwellings and remains of ancient nations do not indicate such heights, and he confessed difficulty resolving it.

responseSource.name: IslamQA 22058; Ibn Hajar, Fath al-Bari on Bukhari 3326

cases.rationale: The Paradise-only reading fails because the hadith's closing line — mankind decreasing in stature 'until now' — is explicitly about earthly history, and the greatest classical commentator on Bukhari conceded the empirical contradiction six centuries ago without answering it. The case's real payload is not the absurd image but the epistemology: this is Bukhari, the collection billed as second only to the Quran, transmitting a checkable falsehood — which reframes every 'but it's sahih' appeal elsewhere (Aisha's age, the fly, the sun's prostration). Keep it as a supporting case, not a lead.

cases.title: 'Aisha was actually 19': the revisionist rescue that mainstream Islam rejects
cases.claim: A popular modern Muslim counter to the Aisha case: the age-nine report comes from a single narrator, Hisham ibn Urwa, whose memory failed in Iraq; and calculations from his sister Asma's age (ten years older, died at 100 in 73 AH) put Aisha at 17-19 at consummation.

sources.name: Yaqeen Institute — 'The Age of Aisha: Rejecting Historical Revisionism and Modernist Presumptions'
ICRAA — 'The Age of Aisha: An Appraisal of the Traditional and Revisionist Perspectives'
WikiIslam — Aisha's Age (chain-by-chain survey)
Sahih Muslim 1422

cases.response: The factual correction — supplied by Muslim scholarship itself: the age reports are not solitary. They come from Aisha in the first person through multiple independent chains (al-Aswad, and other students of Aisha besides Hisham's line, in both Bukhari and Muslim), so impugning Hisham's late-life memory removes nothing. The Asma calculation rests on a report by Ibn Abi al-Zinad born decades after Asma's death — evidentially far weaker than the sahih chains it is invoked to overturn. Yaqeen Institute and ICRAA, mainstream Muslim institutions, both defend age nine and label the 19 thesis methodological revisionism.

responseSource.name: Yaqeen Institute and ICRAA papers cited above

cases.rationale: This entry exists because you will hear the claim: it circulates widely in dawah despite being rejected by Islam's own hadith scholarship. The decisive move in conversation is not to argue the chains yourself but to hand the Muslim their own institutions: Yaqeen's paper is literally titled 'Rejecting Historical Revisionism.' A defense that orthodoxy itself refuses — because accepting it would concede that sahih-graded, multiply-attested reports can be discarded when uncomfortable — dismantles the hadith canon it is trying to protect. Pair with the site's aisha-age case; this is its rebuttal shield.

cases.title: Don't use: 'Muhammad never existed'
cases.claim: The popular version: Muhammad is a myth invented by later Arab empire-builders; there is no evidence he existed (popularized by Robert Spencer's 'Did Muhammad Exist?' and internet mythicism).

sources.name: Patricia Crone — 'What do we actually know about Mohammed?' (openDemocracy)
Institute for Advanced Study — Patricia Crone on Arabia
Jihad Watch — the mythicist claim in the wild (example of the position)

cases.response: The correction: non-Muslim sources name Muhammad within years of his death — the Doctrina Jacobi (c. 634-640) refers to a prophet appearing among the Saracens, and the Armenian chronicle attributed to Sebeos (660s) names him and describes his monotheist preaching. Patricia Crone — the most famous skeptical revisionist of Islamic origins, whom critics love to cite — concluded flatly that there is no doubt Muhammad existed, calling the early external evidence irrefutable.
cases.rationale: Why it backfires: any informed Muslim (or a Google search) produces Crone's quote and the seventh-century references, and your credibility on everything else — Sanaa, qira'at, source criticism — dies with the overclaim, since you have just demonstrated you handle evidence tendentiously. What to say instead: the man existed; the problem is that the detailed biography (sira) rests on sources compiled 150-200 years later (Ibn Ishaq surviving only through Ibn Hisham's recension), which is the honest and devastating source-critical point the site's hadith-chain-of-custody case already makes.

cases.title: Don't use: 'The qibla originally pointed to Petra'
cases.claim: The popular version (Dan Gibson's 'Early Islamic Qiblas'): the earliest mosques face Petra, not Mecca, proving Islam's holy city was originally Petra and the tradition relocated it — therefore the whole origins narrative is fabricated.

sources.name: David A. King — 'From Petra back to Makka: From Pibla back to Qibla'
David A. King — 'The Petra Fallacy: Early mosques do face the Sacred Kaaba in Mecca'
Gibson's response to King (for the claim's own presentation)

cases.response: The correction: David A. King, the leading historian of the science of qibla determination, showed Gibson's method is anachronistic — early mosque builders had no geodesic bearings and oriented mosques by astronomical folk methods (solstitial sunrise/sunset, star risings), which is why orientations scatter; reading modern great-circle bearings back into seventh-century architecture manufactures the Petra alignment. No academic historian of early Islam has adopted the thesis — including the skeptical revisionists critics cite on other points.

responseSource.name: David A. King, 'From Petra back to Makka' and 'The Petra Fallacy'

cases.rationale: Why it backfires: the theory's rejection is not by Muslim apologists but by the very Western academy whose textual criticism the site depends on for Sanaa and the qira'at — lean on Gibson and a prepared opponent uses King to torch your standards of evidence wholesale. What to say instead: nothing is lost by dropping it; the documented problems (Uthman's burning, companion codices, the late sira) are stronger and undisputed.

cases.title: Don't use: 'Muslims worship the Black Stone'
cases.claim: The popular slogan: Muslims claim to oppose idolatry but literally worship a black rock, bowing to it and kissing it.

sources.name: Sahih al-Bukhari 1597 — Umar's words at the Stone
Hadith Encyclopedia — the Umar narration with commentary
Black Stone — Wikipedia

cases.response: The correction: Islam's own canon preempts the charge. Bukhari 1597 — Umar kissed the Stone and said: 'I know that you are a stone and can neither benefit anyone nor harm anyone. Had I not seen Allah's Messenger kissing you, I would not have kissed you.' Muslims venerate the Stone in imitation of Muhammad while explicitly denying it any power; on their own definitions this is not worship, and prayer is directed toward the Kaaba as a direction (qibla), not to it as an object.
cases.rationale: Why it backfires: the Muslim answers with Umar's hadith in one sentence and wins the exchange; worse, the charge invites a tu quoque about crosses, icons, and relics that drags the conversation into symmetry. What to say instead: the site's kaaba-black-stone-pagan-rites case asks the honest version of the question — why a religion founded on smashing paganism retained, unchanged, the pre-Islamic pagan rites of circumambulating and kissing a stone (a continuity Muslim sources themselves document, and which Umar's own bewilderment underlines). Origin, not worship, is the pressure point.

cases.title: Don't use: 'There are 26 (or 31) different Qurans'
cases.claim: The popular version (Speakers' Corner, Jay Smith / Hatun Tash): waving a stack of printed Arabic Qurans — 'here are 26 different Qurans with 93,000 differences; Muslims can't even tell you which one is preserved.'

sources.name: The claim as performed (Hatun Tash / Jay Smith, Speakers' Corner)
Muslim rebuttal — 'Refuting the 26 Qurans Lie'
Yasir Qadhi on the textual history of the Quran (the honest scholarly frame)

cases.response: The correction: the printed editions are the canonical qira'at — transmitted reading traditions (Hafs, Warsh, Qalun, al-Duri, etc.) differing overwhelmingly in pronunciation, orthography, and a bounded set of wording variants, all descending from the Uthmanic consonantal skeleton. The 93,000 figure counts vowel and dialect differences. Calling them '26 different Qurans' is roughly like calling the KJV, NIV, and ESV 'three different Bibles' — a framing Christians reject when Muslims use it, and should not use in reverse.

responseSource.name: Standard qira'at scholarship; conceded even in Muslim rebuttals of Smith

cases.rationale: Why it backfires: a Muslim who has watched one rebuttal video explains qira'at, the numbers deflate on inspection, and the audience concludes the critic didn't understand the material — squandering a real issue. What to say instead: the site already holds the strong version in uthman-burning-companion-codices, sanaa-palimpsest-qiraat, and uthman-standardization-qiraat: why did preservation-by-Allah require Uthman to burn rivals? Why did Ibn Mas'ud reject surahs in today's mushaf? Which of the readings — differing in actual words, not just accent (e.g., Q2:184's variant meanings) — is THE preserved dictation? Precision here wins; the stack of books loses. Note the asymmetry honestly: Islam claims letter-perfect dictation, so even small variants cut deeper against the Quran than against a Bible whose textual history is openly critical.

cases.title: Don't use: 'All Muslims are commanded to lie (taqiyya)'
cases.claim: The popular version: taqiyya is a general Islamic commandment to deceive unbelievers, so nothing any Muslim says — in dialogue, in politics, in interfaith settings — can be trusted.

sources.name: Taqiyya — Wikipedia (doctrine overview and scope)
Sahih al-Bukhari 3030 — 'War is deceit'
This site — taqiyya-deception (the honest version of the doctrine)

cases.response: The correction: classical taqiyya is a dispensation, not a command — concealment of one's faith under compulsion or mortal danger (Quran 16:106; 3:28's 'unless you fear them'), elaborated chiefly in Shia jurisprudence under Sunni persecution. Ordinary Islamic ethics condemns lying. The genuine residue is narrower and documented: deception sanctioned in warfare ('war is deceit,' Bukhari 3030) and episodes like the sanctioned deception of Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf — which is what this site's taqiyya case presents.

responseSource.name: Classical fiqh of taqiyya; this site's taqiyya-deception case

cases.rationale: Why it backfires: the overclaim is unfalsifiable conspiracy logic — if every Muslim denial is itself taqiyya, no evidence can ever count against you, and thoughtful listeners recognize the move and discount everything else you say. It also misstates the doctrine's actual scope, which a Muslim can demonstrate in seconds. What to say instead: the precise version — Islam permits concealment under persecution and sanctions deception in war, and Muhammad personally authorized deceptive assassination — is documented, damaging, and defensible. Accusing your specific interlocutor of lying is both unwarranted and conversation-ending.

cases.title: Don't use: 'The Quran promises 72 virgins'
cases.claim: The popular version: 'the Quran promises martyrs 72 virgins in paradise.'

sources.name: Jami at-Tirmidhi 1663 — the six rewards of the martyr, including seventy-two wives
Abu Amina Elias — 'Seventy two virgins in Paradise?'
WikiIslam — Authenticity of 72 Virgins Hadith
SeekersGuidance — '72 Virgins for Martyrs' (Muslim treatment)

cases.response: The correction: the number 72 appears nowhere in the Quran. The Quran promises houris — created, wide-eyed, virginal companions (56:22-24, 44:54, 55:56, 78:33) — without a count. The 72 figure is hadith: Jami at-Tirmidhi 1663 lists among the martyr's six rewards marriage to 'seventy-two wives from al-hur al-'ayn' (wives, not 'virgins,' in the wording), a report graded sahih/hasan in mainstream collections but still a hadith claim, not a Quranic one.
cases.rationale: Why it backfires: say 'the Quran promises 72 virgins' and the Muslim truthfully replies 'no it doesn't' — you lose on a citation error and the real point escapes with it. The substance survives precision: the Quran's paradise is explicitly material and sexual (the site's houris-material-paradise case), and the 72-wives detail for martyrs IS in a sahih-graded hadith — cite it as Tirmidhi 1663 and the technicality defense evaporates. Precision converts a losing slogan into an unanswerable citation.
